SEC26A-01.note: Subject 'the young' is a plural nominalized adjective -> 'are'; the begging belongs to the nestlings -> 'their'. 'Its' tempts if read as the nest/brood.

SEC26A-02.note: 'Each' is singular despite 'patients'/'wards'; past progressive required by 'when the sponsor put the trial on hold'. 'Were keeping' attracts via plural nouns.

SEC26A-03.note: Many trays exist, so 'kept nearest the freezer's door' is restrictive and takes no commas. B tempts by pairing with the comma already after 'door' (which actually belongs to the 'where' clause); C (dash/comma mismatch) and D (comma inside the participle phrase) are rejectable on sight.

SEC26A-04.note: Singular 'ointment' plus 'since ... voted last spring' requires present perfect 'has been prescribed'. 'Was prescribed' tempts on the past-tense cue.

SEC26A-05.note: Plural 'needles' -> 'are'; agent is the bacteria -> 'them'. Singular 'pine' right before the blank attracts 'is' and 'it'.

SEC26A-06.note: 'The oats were seldom ... rotten enough to discard': 'were' + predicate adjective, separated by a long interrupter; 'have seldom ... rotten' lacks 'been' and present perfect clashes with the past record. 'Oats' as plural defeats 'has/was'.

SEC26A-07.note: Two independent clauses; the second is a new point (catgut's other market), not an explanation, so a period, not a colon. B is a strong garden path (appositive reading) but leaves 'had' without a clause boundary. D is the closest rival: colon between independent clauses is legal only when the second elaborates the first, which it does not here.

SEC26A-08.note: Singular 'pancreas' and generic present ('unless the animals receive') -> 'is damaged'. Plural 'mice' attracts 'are'; the later past 'went on' attracts 'was'.

SEC26A-09.note: The cooperative's members' collective harvest, contrasted with the founder's own trees -> plural possessive 'growers''. 'Grower's' tempts but no single grower is identified.

SEC26A-10.note: Intransitive 'spray' ends the introductory clause; 'the vines growing ...' is the main subject. A and B are garden paths that absorb 'the vines' as spray's object, leaving 'were showing' subjectless; D puts a semicolon after a dependent clause.

SEC26B-01.note: Plural 'engineers' -> 'have'; what was reconstructed is the single 'last status report' -> 'it'. Plural 'stations'/'dish ... each' and the long distance to the antecedent make 'them' attractive.

SEC26B-02.note: Singular 'front' (not 'crevasses'/'currents') and present 'whenever ... drain' -> 'is prone'. 'Was' tempts from 'over three summers' and 'captured'.

SEC26B-03.note: Two independent clauses; a colon already introduces the list of defects, so the boundary takes a semicolon, not a second colon. A tempts as an appositive ('a faint gray line, the fainter mark ...') but leaves 'tore open' as a splice.

SEC26B-04.note: Plural 'segments'; the definite past time 'on the evening of the ... open house' rules out present perfect -> 'were cleaned'. Singular 'mirror's' attracts 'was/has'.

SEC26B-05.note: Ellipsis: 'the steel tapes ... do [lengthen]', a plural auxiliary standing for 'lengthens' in the contrast. 'Were' tempts from 'nineteenth-century' but there is no elided adjective/participle for it to carry; 'does/was' fail on number.

SEC26B-06.note: Singular 'receiver' (not 'twin domes') -> 'is'; it tracks the 'grains' -> 'them'. 'Are' attracted by 'domes', 'it' by 'receiver'.

SEC26B-07.note: 'As the crew blasted the ridge,' closes the introductory clause; 'loosened boulders ... fell' is the main clause. A garden-paths into 'the ridge loosened boulders', which leaves 'fell' orphaned; B lacks the needed comma; C semicolon after a dependent clause.

SEC26B-08.note: Plural 'staves' and past 'while ... slowly cooled' -> 'were being replaced'. Singular 'hearth'/'wall' attract 'was'; the generic present of the first sentence attracts 'are'.

SEC26B-09.note: Single bunk and every page 'in the same hand' -> one observer -> singular possessive 'observer's'. 'Observers'' tempts for readers who miss the context clue in the previous sentence.

SEC26B-10.note: A complex list whose later item boundary is already a semicolon ('nucleus; and') -> semicolon here too. Matching the printed semicolon decides it; D (no mark) is struck on sight.
SEC26B-10.drop_reason: Easy for the hard route: the key is decided by copying the semicolon already printed in the parallel list slot ('nucleus; and'), with no structural parsing needed.

SEC26C-01.note: Singular 'curtain' -> 'was'; neglected by the three painters -> 'them'. Plural 'painters'/'backdrops' attract 'were'; 'it' tempts as a reflex singular.

SEC26C-02.note: 'The illiterate' is a plural nominalized adjective (the illiterate people), and 'since ... discarded' requires present perfect -> 'have been invisible'. 'Has been' is the strong lure for readers who treat 'the illiterate' as a singular mass noun.

SEC26C-03.note: Plural 'copes' and a past event ('on the eve of the great fire') -> 'were removed'. Singular 'inventory'/'vestment' and the present 'is worn' attract the other forms.

SEC26C-04.note: Colon after an independent clause introducing what the 'decisive clue' was. A is a comma splice; B fused; D ('sight the,') garbled on sight.

SEC26C-05.note: Plural 'copyists' and interrupted past action ('when floodwaters ... spread') -> 'were decorating'. Singular 'scriptorium' attracts 'was'; 'have decorated' fails the tense.

SEC26C-06.note: Singular 'editor' -> 'was'; the object revised is the novel's final chapter (cutting digressions about the hero's childhood) -> 'it'. 'Sonnets' right before the blank lures both 'were' and 'them'.

SEC26C-07.note: Singular 'toll' adjacent to the blank, past event at the first patron's funeral -> 'was audible'. Present 'carries' in sentence 1 is the only lure.

SEC26C-08.note: Singular 'restorer' (not 'paintings') and a past frame 'before the councillors quit paying' -> 'was cleaning'. 'Has been cleaning' fails against the completed past.

SEC26C-09.note: He had only one letter book ('that one volume'), so the participle phrase is nonrestrictive -> comma. B is the strong lure (restrictive reading is grammatical in isolation, and the uniqueness clue sits in the next sentence); D (comma inside the participle phrase) struck on sight; C makes a fragment.

SEC26C-10.convention: Generic definite singular ('the apprentice' as the role, parallel to 'the master printer') with past-tense 'cast', which is identical to the present plural form; the sentence is past ('set', 'pulled').
SEC26C-10.note: Intended: plural 'apprentices' because a master trained three or four boys at a time. But 'In such a shop the apprentice cast new letters ... while the master printer set the pages and pulled the proofs' is a grammatical past-tense generic singular, so B is defensible; the number clue is semantic, not grammatical.
SEC26C-10.drop_reason: B ('the apprentice cast ...') is a grammatical past-tense generic singular parallel to 'the master printer'; the author's own explanation concedes it forms a grammatical clause, so the item is decided by a semantic inference from a later sentence rather than by a convention.

SEC26D-01.note: Singular 'diner' -> 'judges'; what is judged is the one 'oddly precise price' -> 'it'. Plural 'prices' attracts 'them'.

SEC26D-02.note: Singular 'bilingualism' adjacent to the blank; a completed past period ('at the height of the harbor's grain trade', trade later collapsed) -> 'was widespread'. Present perfect fails the definite past.

SEC26D-03.note: The town had only one newspaper (no other press in the valley), so 'the Sentinel' is a nonrestrictive appositive; a single dash introducing it to the end of the sentence is correct (the later comma belongs to the 'whose' clause). A (restrictive, no punctuation) is the strong lure; C makes a fragment; D garbled.

SEC26D-04.note: Plural 'tenants'; present tense locked by 'as long as that increase stays' -> 'are accepting'. The parenthetical past 'the interviewers found' lures backshift to 'were accepting'.

SEC26D-05.note: Singular 'study' (not 'interns'/'classmates') and 'since that first recruitment drive' -> 'has been following'.

SEC26D-06.note: Singular 'suffix' (not 'verbs'/'schools') -> 'has never ... fully disappeared' (present perfect with a past participle; 'is ... disappeared' is not standard).

SEC26D-07.note: Plural 'teams' -> 'have'; the wording belongs to the questionnaire -> 'its'. 'Their' tempts as matching the plural subject; singular 'north'/'office' lures 'has'.

SEC26D-08.note: Plural 'volunteers' (not 'desk'/'grant') and 'since the school's closure', far after the blank -> 'have coached'. 'Were coaching' tempts if the 'since' phrase is missed.

SEC26D-09.convention: A colon may introduce a final appositive/explanatory noun phrase after a complete independent clause (Chicago 6.65; 'He had one ally: the dog').
SEC26D-09.note: Intended: comma before the end-of-sentence appositive 'the widow of the shop's first foreman ...'. But the clause before the blank is independent and what follows is a renaming noun phrase running to the end, so the colon (B) is also standard. Separately, 'foreman trained in double-entry accounts by her own father' reads as modifying the foreman, a misplaced-modifier flaw in the passage itself.
SEC26D-09.drop_reason: The colon (B) is also standard for a sentence-final amplifying noun phrase after a complete independent clause, and the passage itself contains a misplaced modifier ('foreman trained ... by her own father' reads as the foreman being trained), so the stimulus is not clean edited English.

SEC26D-10.note: 'Rules' is the main verb (singular) and the charter assigns the duty to 'a lone appointee' -> 'parliamentarian'. Possessive options lure a noun reading of 'rules', which leaves the first clause without a verb.

tells: Agreement attractor polarity: in 2x2 number items the noun printed immediately before the blank usually has the OPPOSITE number to the key (A-02 wards, A-05 pine, A-08 mice, B-06 domes, B-08 hearth, C-05 scriptorium, C-06 sonnets, C-08 paintings, D-05 classmates, D-06 verbs, D-07 north, D-08 desk). Counterexamples exist (SEC26A-01 broods, SEC26B-01 stations), which weakens but does not remove the heuristic 'never agree with the adjacent noun'.

'since' in the sentence keys present perfect every time it appears (SEC26A-04, SEC26C-02, SEC26D-05, SEC26D-08); otherwise present perfect loses except SEC26D-06. That is the rule itself, but it is applied mechanically with the same 'since + past event' cue each time.
No-punctuation option loses on 9 of 10 boundary/punctuation items (wins only SEC26A-03).
Trailing-comma-after-second-word option ('tray kept,', 'book filled,', 'sight the,', 'newspaper the,') loses 4 of 5; it is the key only in SEC26B-07.

Possessive items each key a different form once (SEC26A-09 plural possessive, SEC26B-09 singular possessive, SEC26C-10 plural, SEC26D-10 singular), and in all four the number clue sits in a sentence outside the blank's sentence: once a test-taker learns to look for the 'one person / many people' sentence the four become identical.
Verb-pronoun 2x2 items are balanced (4 matched-number keys, 4 mismatched), so no letter or pairing tell there.
near_duplicates: restrictive versus nonrestrictive participle after a noun, mirrored keys
introductory clause garden path where the verb could absorb the following noun
sentence boundary before 'the' after a noun, period/semicolon/colon choice
appositive after a name or noun, punctuation choice
noun number and possessive decided by a context sentence elsewhere in the passage
passive verb plus 'by them/it' agent pronoun 2x2
verb number crossed with object or possessive pronoun number
number crossed with present perfect versus past, decided by 'since'
number crossed with past progressive, decided by a when/while/before clause

phase2_note: All 40 keys match my cold answers (0 cold misses) and all 40 explanations give a working path. SEC26A-07's explanation also cites the later colon ('market: the string makers'), which I had missed and which makes the period stronger. Three drops recommended: SEC26C-10 and SEC26D-09 (a second defensible option, as flagged in phase 1) and SEC26B-10 (decided by matching a printed mark). Borderline but kept: SEC26C-07 and SEC26D-02 are easy, with the subject next to the blank and weak distractors.
